claim: Subjects were occasionally asked (every 12 to 18 sounds) to report an explicit discrete prediction about the forthcoming stimulus using one of two buttons.

source: Each block presented 400 to 409 stimuli and lasted for about 10 min.

claim: The experiment was split into four different conditions characterized by different first-order transition probabilities.
source: The four different conditions were characterized by different first-order transition probabilities (see Figure 1B): a condition with a frequency bias (i.e. p(A|B) = 1/3 and p(B|A) = 2/3 which led to p(A) = 1/3 and p(alt.) = 4/9), a condition with a repetition bias (i.e. p(A|B) = p(B|A) = 1/3 which led to p(A) = 1/2 and p(alt.) = 1/3), a condition with an alternation bias (i.e. p(A|B) = p(B|A) = 2/3 which led to p(A) = 1/2 and p(alt.) = 2/3) and a fully stochastic condition devoted of any bias (i.e. p(A|B) = p(B|A) = 1/2 which led to p(A) = 1/2 and p(alt.) = 1/2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the four experimental conditions with their transition probabilities.

claim: Brain activity was recorded using a 306 channels whole-head Elekta Neuromag MEG system with an acquisition sampling rate of 1 kHz.
source: Subjects' brain activity was recorded using a 306 channels (102 triplets of sensors each composed of 1 magnetometer and two orthogonal planar gradiometers) whole-head Elekta Neuromag MEG system with an acquisition sampling rate of 1 kHz and hardware bandpass filtering between 0.1 and 330 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the MEG recording system and parameters.

claim: The grand-averaged MEG responses evoked by the sounds revealed four distinct canonical components: M50, M150, M250, and M3/slow-wave.
source: The grand-averaged MEG responses evoked by the sounds revealed four distinct canonical components (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2): three early responses (M50, M150 and M250 components) characterized by topographies plausibly arising from bilateral auditory cortex (Chait et al., 2007; Strauss et al., 2015) and a late response associated with the classical P300/slow-wave topography (Wacongne et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the four MEG components observed, with references to prior literature.

claim: In the frequency-biased condition, rare A items elicited larger responses than frequent B items (significant between 227 and 910 ms post-sound onset).
source: In the frequency-biased condition, rare A items were overall less frequent than frequent B items and, as expected, rare items elicited larger responses than frequent ones (significant between 227 and 910 ms post-sound onset, see Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical finding with time window and references to figures.

claim: In the repetition-biased condition, rare alternations evoked significantly larger signals than frequent repetitions (significant between 391 and 633 ms post-sound onset).
source: In the repetition-biased condition, repetitions, that is XX = AA or BB, were overall more frequent than alternations, that is XY = AB or BA; brain signals also reflected this bias, showing increased activity for rare alternations as compared to frequent repetitions (significant between 391 and 633 ms post-sound onset, see Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical finding with time window and references to figures.

claim: In the alternation-biased condition, brain signals were larger for rare repetitions than frequent alternations (significant between 176 and 371 ms post-sound onset).
source: In the alternation-biased condition, in which alternations are overall more frequent than repetitions, we found a reversal of the effect compared to the repetition-biased condition. Brain signals were larger for rare repetitions than frequent alternations (significant between 176 and 371 ms post-sound onset, see Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical finding with time window and references to figures.

claim: In the fully stochastic condition, no significant difference was found for the A – B contrast or for the repetition – alternation contrast.
source: Finally, in the fully stochastic condition, there was no global bias regarding item or alternation frequencies: there were as many As as Bs and as many repetitions as alternations. Accordingly, no significant difference was found, neither for the A – B contrast (see first row in Figure 2A) nor for the repetition – alternation one (see first row in Figure 2B).
